questions.question_text:
A quantity satisfies $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$.
When $Q=80$ litres, the quantity is increasing at $6$ litres per hour.
Find $k$.

options.why: Attached a negative sign although the quantity is increasing, so $k>0$.
Divided $Q$ by the rate instead of the rate by $Q$.
Divided $Q$ by the rate and also attached a negative sign to an increasing quantity.

questions.question_text:
The mass $M$ of a sample decreases at a rate proportional to the mass present, with constant of proportionality $0.12$.
Which differential equation models this?

options.why: Used a positive constant, which models growth rather than a decreasing mass.
Made the rate proportional to the time rather than to the amount present.
Made the rate proportional to the time and also used a positive constant.

questions.solution_text:
The rate is proportional to the amount $M$, so $\dfrac{dM}{dt}=kM$.
The mass is decreasing, so $k$ is negative.
$\dfrac{dM}{dt}=-0.12M$

questions.question_text:
A quantity is given by $Q=-300e^{0.2t}$.
Which statement about this model is correct?

options.text: $k=0.2>0$, and because $A<0$ the quantity is negative and becomes more negative as $t$ increases.
$k=0.2>0$, so the quantity increases towards larger and larger positive values.
options.why: Read $k>0$ as meaning $Q$ must rise, ignoring the negative value of $A$.

options.text: $k=-0.2<0$, so the quantity decays towards zero.
options.why: Took the minus sign from $A$ and attached it to $k$ instead.

options.text: Because $A<0$, the value of $k$ must also be negative, so this is decay.
options.why: Assumed the sign of $A$ determines the sign of $k$; the two are independent.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=-300e^{0.2t}$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=-60e^{0.2t}$
$=0.2\left(-300e^{0.2t}\right)$
$=0.2Q$
$k=0.2>0$
$A=-300<0$, so $Q<0$ for all $t$, and since $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}<0$ the quantity becomes more negative as $t$ increases.

questions.question_text: Which of these functions does NOT satisfy $\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=kQ$ for any constant $k$?

options.why: This does satisfy the equation, with $k=0.5$.
A negative value of $A$ still satisfies the equation, with $k=0.5$.
This does satisfy the equation, with $k=9$; the roles of $A$ and $k$ are simply swapped.

questions.solution_text:
$Q=9e^{0.5t}+2$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=4.5e^{0.5t}$
$9e^{0.5t}=Q-2$
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt}=0.5\left(Q-2\right)$
$=0.5Q-1$
This is not a constant multiple of $Q$, so no value of $k$ works.
